justification_text:
My point estimates across all three horizons were anchored primarily to the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, with only modest drift built in. For the 1-day estimate, I leaned heavily on recent price momentum and mean-reversion tendencies, expecting little meaningful deviation from the last observed price. At the 1-week horizon, I introduced a slight upward tilt reflecting a marginally positive trend bias, while at the 1-month horizon I allowed for a somewhat larger drift, consistent with a slow-moving bullish baseline. The relatively small differences between the three point estimates reflect my view that the asset was in a consolidation phase without strong directional catalysts immediately visible, so the central expectation was essentially flat to slightly higher across all horizons.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to historical realized volatility, which I scaled up proportionally with the square root of time — a standard approach that acknowledges uncertainty compounds as the forecast horizon extends. At one day, the interval is tight because intraday and overnight volatility is relatively bounded under normal conditions. By one week, macro data releases, sentiment shifts, and liquidity fluctuations all add meaningful uncertainty. By one month, the interval widens substantially to capture the full range of potential trend changes, earnings or economic surprises, and broader market regime shifts. I also applied a modest fat-tail adjustment to each interval, recognizing that financial returns are not perfectly normally distributed.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected negative macro shock — such as a sharp deterioration in credit conditions, a geopolitical escalation, or a surprise central bank policy shift — could drive prices well below the lower bound even at the 1-day horizon. A sudden liquidity event or forced deleveraging in related markets could amplify moves beyond what historical volatility alone would suggest. On the upside, a strong positive catalyst such as better-than-expected economic data, a dovish policy surprise, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices above the upper bounds, particularly at the shorter horizons where the intervals are narrowest. The 1-month interval, while wide, would still be breached under a sustained trend reversal or a structural market repricing event.
